About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Food Processing Technology Years
11–13 of the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Food Processing Technology Years 11–13
is still in development. Once that is completed, Food Processing Technology Years
11–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum
Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Food Processing Technology Years 11–13 will be required to start using it
in Year 11 from 1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from
1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  Students are taught the technological knowledge and skills to develop food                     Food Processing Technology leads to pathways in food process engineering,
  products through the technology design framework. Students are taught about                    food science, food technology, product design, hospitality, biotechnology, and
  the performance properties of ingredients, societal, economic, ethical, cultural               health.
  and environmental considerations to make informed decisions about ingredient
  selections, processing equipment, processes, and sustainable practices, to
  develop and create innovative food products addressing societal needs or
  emerging opportunities. They are taught how to apply processing methods and
  techniques such as processing methods, codes of practice, preservation, and
  quality control, using creative problem-solving and technological thinking to
  produce fit-for-purpose outcomes.

In Food Processing Technology students are taught food science concepts including
biotechnology, chemistry, microbiology, and nutrition. They apply this knowledge to
the development of food products through human-centred design, systems thinking,
food safety, sustainability, and consideration of consumer needs.

Food Processing Technology provides students with the knowledge and practices to
explore food science problems and opportunities, manage uncertainty, and refine
outcomes using in-depth cycles of noticing, defining, ideating, analysing, developing,
creating, and evaluating design outcomes. This disciplinary knowledge enables
students to evaluate and communicate, in written form, the broader impacts of food
production processing and the role of stakeholders in the design process.

As students progress through Year 11–13, they are supported to develop their ability
to use an iterative, non-linear, and interdisciplinary technology framework, view failure
and malfunction as critical data points in the design process and analyse feedback
loops from AI-supported and human sources to drive the evolution of a design over
time. They consider how technological outcomes are shaped by the lived
experiences, diverse perspectives, and collective agency of those who will use or be
impacted by the solution.

 Disciplinary writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within Food Processing Technology.
 In Food Processing Technology, writing is an analytical and reflective practice that enables students to develop and refine ideas through description, explanation, and evaluation
 of food products and processing methods, while communicating informed understanding.

In Year 13, students explore innovative food products and evaluate trade-offs
and competing considerations to establish technical feasibility, social
acceptability, and fitness for purpose in the broadest sense. The complexity at
this level comes from managing multiple considerations rather than solely from
the complexity of the food product itself. Learning at this level does not require
professional food science or commercial manufacturing expertise.
